topStories.headline: Marina Safeway Tower Clears Key Planning Hurdle as Neighborhood Fight Intensifies
topStories.dek: San Francisco's planning director has rejected Supervisor Sherrill's last-ditch legal challenges to the 848-unit Align Real Estate proposal, moving the project closer to approval.
topStories.body:
The battle over the Marina Safeway at 15 Marina Boulevard entered a decisive new phase this week, after San Francisco Planning Director Sarah Dennis Phillips formally struck down arguments from District 2 Supervisor Stephen Sherrill that the project failed to meet state law eligibility requirements. In a July 20 letter, Phillips determined that the property is not on the state's Cortese List of hazardous waste sites, is not in an earthquake fault zone, and is not in a federally designated flood hazard area — clearing the main legal obstacles that opponents had raised to block the development under AB 2011.

Developer Align Real Estate, filing on behalf of property owner Albertsons Companies (which owns Safeway), has updated its plans to reduce the towers from 25 and 22 stories to 22 and 18 stories while simultaneously increasing the total residential count from 790 to 848 units. The revised proposal would include 254 studios, 268 one-bedrooms, 212 two-bedrooms, and 114 three-bedrooms across nearly 990,000 square feet of total development, along with a rebuilt Safeway store on the ground floor.

The project has galvanized neighborhood opposition and drawn over 300 residents to a packed town hall at Fort Mason. Marina Community Association president Erin Roach helped organize the meeting and has publicly stated that the group supports housing at the site but objects to the scale. Mayor Daniel Lurie has also opposed the project, and his office confirmed it is still not prepared to support the revised proposal.

Opposition to the project has now spilled into broader California politics. A coalition has aligned around a proposed initiative dubbed the Balanced Housing Act, which would amend the California constitution to prohibit the state from imposing housing growth mandates on cities lacking the infrastructure to absorb new residents. The coalition aims to qualify the measure for the November 2030 ballot. A final planning decision on the Safeway project could come within months.

topStories.headline: Upper Fillmore Restaurant Wave Grows: Michelin-Starred Thai Chef Joins Korean BBQ Newcomer
topStories.dek: Chef Pim Techamuanvivit of Kin Khao and Nari is taking over the former Starbucks at 2222 Fillmore, adding a second high-profile opening to the Pacific Heights corridor's ongoing transformation.
topStories.body:
Upper Fillmore Street's restaurant renaissance claimed a second major tenant this week, as SFist reported that chef Pim Techamuanvivit — known for the Michelin-starred Kin Khao and Nari — is planning a new restaurant at 2222 Fillmore Street, the former Starbucks location between Clay and Sacramento streets. The working title is Khao Soi Ya, signaling a focus on the Thai curry noodle soup khao soi, building on Techamuanvivit's 2024 pop-up concept of the same name.

The news comes alongside the ongoing build-out of Monami, an upscale Korean barbecue restaurant from Junsoo and Hyunyoung Bae — the founders of Michelin-starred SSAL on upper Polk Street — who are taking over the long-vacant former Noosh space at 2001 Fillmore. Chef Junsoo Bae has described the concept as a Korean barbecue version of House of Prime Rib, with both an à la carte menu and a tasting menu format. Monami is targeting a fall 2026 opening.

Both projects are part of a broader neighborhood transformation anchored by billionaire venture capitalist Neil Mehta, who has purchased several buildings along a stretch of upper Fillmore, including the historic Clay Theatre. The Clay is undergoing a renovation modeled after New York's Metrograph arthouse cinema concept, with completion expected in 2027. The New Fillmore, a neighborhood publication covering Pacific Heights, noted that anticipation for the Clay's return is running high among long-time residents.

topStories.headline: District 2 Supervisor Race Heads to November with Safeway Project as Central Issue
topStories.dek: The November 3 general election for the Marina-Pacific Heights supervisor seat is shaping up as a referendum on housing development, neighborhood character, and state housing law.
topStories.body:
San Francisco's District 2 — encompassing the Marina, Pacific Heights, Cow Hollow, and Presidio Heights — is heading into a November 3 general election for a full four-year supervisor term, with the Marina Safeway housing controversy looming large over the race. Incumbent Stephen Sherrill, appointed to the seat in December 2024 after Catherine Stefani was elected to the California State Assembly, won a June 2 special election but faces a fresh contest this fall.

Sherrill has publicly opposed the Align Real Estate Safeway redevelopment project and sent letters to the city's planning department raising legal challenges, all of which were ultimately rejected by Planning Director Sarah Dennis Phillips. His opponent Lori Brooke, co-founder of Neighborhoods United SF, also opposed the project and appeared alongside Sherrill at a packed Fort Mason town hall on the issue in late July.

The District 2 race has attracted significant fundraising, with Sherrill leading in campaign finance totals ahead of the June primary. The seat is one of five even-numbered district seats on the 11-member Board of Supervisors up for election on November 3, 2026. Voters are expected to cast ballots using ranked-choice voting.

moreNews.headline: Waterfront Takes Center Stage as Marina's Summer Social Gravity Shifts
moreNews.body: A summer guide published by a local real estate blogger captures what many Marina and Cow Hollow residents have noticed: the neighborhood's social center has migrated from Chestnut and Union streets toward the waterfront. Presidio Tunnel Tops, now in its fourth programmed summer season, Fort Mason's monthly night market, and Crissy Field's open green spaces are drawing residents and visitors away from the commercial corridors and onto the bay-facing parklands. The Presidio is also ramping up programming ahead of the 250th anniversary of the founding of El Presidio de San Francisco on September 17, 1776.

moreNews.headline: Nisei Soldier Experience Exhibition Open at Presidio Through August 31
moreNews.body: The Military Intelligence Service Historic Learning Center at 640 Mason Street in the Presidio is hosting 'I Am An American: The Nisei Soldier Experience,' presented by the National Japanese American Historical Society with the Presidio Trust. The exhibition is open Fridays through Tuesdays through August 31, from 12 to 5 p.m. Admission is free for veterans, children 12 and under, and NJAHS members; $15 for all others.

moreNews.headline: Zoox Robotaxi Service Expands into Marina and Pacific Heights
moreNews.body: Amazon-owned autonomous vehicle company Zoox expanded its San Francisco service area earlier this year to include the Marina, Pacific Heights, North Beach, Chinatown, and the Embarcadero corridor — quadrupling its previous footprint. The aloe-green robotaxis are currently available to Zoox employees, their friends and family, and riders from a public waitlist. The company has said it is focused on expanding in areas where most ride-hailing activity takes place before moving into more residential neighborhoods.
